paper_title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazons SQID and Wayfairs WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, large number of them pick the same wrong product. 1. Introduction Shopping is becoming an increasingly agentic task. Assistants built on large language models (LLMs) now search catalogs, compare listings and place orders with little human review [2, 12, 42]. Two properties of such an agent matter to the person it acts for: whether its choice is preferable, and whether it is overconfident in its decision. For the latter, if an agent is overconfident, it may quietly buy the wrong thing, while if it is well-calibrated (by which we mean models self-reported confidence is close to its true reliability), it can hand the decision back to the user when it is unsure. Modern frontier LLMs with which these agents are implemented now possess an explicit reasoning effort control. Reasoning effort allows users to request low, medium or high effort. At higher reasoning efforts, model spends correspondingly more tokens thinking before it answers [9, 29]. On math and coding benchmarks this increase in inferencetime compute is shown to improve accuracy [22, 36]. However, whether inference-time scaling using longer thinking improves everyday decisions like shopping whose difficulty lies in reading listing carefully rather than in multistep derivation is less clear [7, 37], and whether it improves calibration is largely untested. Thus, we will study the effects of increased reasoning effort in agentic shopping using three datasets: (I) The WebShop [42] environment, which contains Amazon product listings with images of the product and text containing the product data; (II) the Amazon Shopping Queries dataset with SQID images [1, 35], multimodal dataset with image information and visual embeddings for different Amazon products along with associated search queries in text form; and (III) the Wayfair WANDS [8] dataset, text-only benchmark where each product contains title, some features, and description. As we will describe later (Sec. 3), in our experiments, we will also isolate the decision-making part of the shopping task from the search and navigation part. From our experiments, we first find in Sec. 4.2 that moving from low to high effort changes correctness by only small amount for any LLM: Only three models improve their success rate by statistically significant amount in WebShop, and even fewer models show the same improvements in the other two datasets. However, we find that the same change in effort raises stated confidence significantly for nine of ten models in WebShop, five of ten models in SQID, and six in WANDS, so raising reasoning level delivers more confidence without corresponding correctness. Then, we find in Sec. 4.3 that calibration is almost entirely model-dependent: there doesnt seem to be any correlation between calibration metrics like ECE, Brier scores, or AUROC (defined later 1 in Sec. 3.3) across models regardless of reasoning effort. Finally, as we will show in Sec. 4.4, mistakes are correlated across different models: the number of models wrong on any given task is much more concentrated than what we would expect from an independent-models baseline. Moreover, when several models err on the same task, they typically choose the same incorrect product. Main Contributions. Thus, this paper makes three contributions: (I) We show that reasoning effort is largely ineffective for improving shopping decisions but does tend to make models more confident (Sec. 4.2). (II) We show some models are consistently much more confident, but not more accurate, than other models (Sec. 4.3). (III) We provide cross-model benchmarking framework of frontier LLM shopping agents, covering calibration, market concentration, and reasoning effort across ten models and three datasets (Sec. 3.1). 2. Related Work LLM agents for shopping. WebShop [42] introduced simulated store with 1.18M real products and human instructions and remains the standard testbed for language agents that search, browse and buy; later web-agent benchmarks [11, 43] and shopping suites [20] broadened the task mix. These works report end-to-end success, where navigation and decision failures are confounded. Allouah et al. [2] evaluate agents as economic actors and document strong concentration of demand on few products and sensitivity to listing position, and El Housni and Ibn Brahim [12] model the assistant as mediating layer between retailer and customer and show that it materially changes optimal assortments and revenue. In this paper, we take the complementary approach of investigating the agents role as buyer whose decision must be judged, and isolate that decision by fixing the choice set, so every error is attributable to product judgment and conditions are compared on identical inputs. This approach was also advocated for by the recent concurrent work of Candogan [6], which argues that an agent can complete purchase while making poor choice for its user, and evaluates commercial shopping agents on fixed choice sets drawn from retail catalog against customers with known preferences: Candogan finds that decision quality degrades sharply as choice sets grow and preferences are only partially communicated. Confidence and calibration of LLMs. Classic calibration work in vision [17, 28] measured the gap between classifiers probability and its accuracy. For LLMs, confidence is usually elicited verbally [23, 38, 41] or read from token probabilities [21]; verbalized confidence is typically overconfident, clustered at few round values, and only moderately discriminative, as in people [26, 39]. In this paper, we follow this literature in evaluating verbalized confidence with ECE, Brier score and AUROC (defined in Sec. 3.3), but ask how it responds to reasoning-effort control that was not yet widely adopted (or did not yet exist) when most of the just-mentioned literature was written. Test-time compute and reasoning effort. Chain-of-thought prompting [40] and reinforcement-trained reasoning models [9, 29] established that spending more tokens at inference time can raise accuracy, and scaling studies [27, 36] characterized the trade-off. That benefit is typically concentrated in mathematical and symbolic tasks [37], and long reasoning can be wasteful on easy problems [7]. In this paper, we measure the effect of reasoning effort on agentic shopping in particular and ask whether it changes not only accuracy but also the models own assessment of that accuracy. Shared errors across models. Error consistency between classifiers has been studied in vision as signature of shared inductive biases [13, 24], and recent work warns that increasingly similar LLMs undermine oversight schemes that rely on inter-model disagreement [14]. In this paper, we quantify error sharing in an agentic shopping setting against an explicit independence baseline and show that it is large and insensitive to the thinking effort. 3. Data and Methods 3.1. Three datasets (2 multimodal and 1 text) All experiments in this study have the same form: shopping query, fixed and shuffled list of ten candidate products, and exactly one candidate that is correct. Presenting the full list removes search and navigation from the experiment, so every model at every effort level decides on identical evidence, and it allows paired analysis in which each model is compared with itself, task by task, across effort levels. The three dataset sources differ in where the query and products come from and in how correct is defined. We describe each dataset below and provide summary in Tab. S1 in the Supplement. WebShop. WebShop [42] is multimodal (images with text) dataset whose instructions name product type and set of required attributes, option values and price ceiling (I need long-lasting antiperspirant deodorant for women, 2.6 ounce, under $40). Its reward function (written as Python function) scores any productoption choice on scale of 0 to 1 on whether the chosen products attribute, option and price match what was stated in the query (see Sec. 3 of [42]). choice is correct if and only if it earns the maximum reward of 1. On top of the WebShop environment, we build the following tasks for our experiments: For each given query from the original WebShop test set, we take target product (that has reward 1 given the query), and we identify nine other products that (a) are the same kind of product or sharing the targets most specific category, (b) cannot reach perfect reward under any option choice and (c) fail at least one requirement under lenient paraphrase check. Each product carries its title, seeded price, bullet features, description, selectable options and main image. 2 Instructions with fewer than nine such distractors (which we define as products that fulfill the above three requirements) are skipped, leaving 496 tasks (examples in Sec. H, Tab. S14 in the Supplement). Amazon SQID. SQID [1, 35] combines real Amazon search queries with human judgment-based answers. It is constructed from an earlier Amazon Shopping Queries (ASQ) dataset [35], which contains set of queries and corresponding set of products for each query. ASQ pairs each query with list of products that annotators labeled Exact (satisfies every specification in the query), Substitute (fails some specification but could serve the same purpose), Complement (would be used together with an Exact product) or Irrelevant. The authors of the original ASQ [35] call this ESCI labeling, for Exact, Substitute, Complement, Irrelevant. SQID adds product image for most of these products, making it multimodal dataset. Queries are short and typed the way shoppers type them (running sunglasses for men, makita inflator 18v, kids sleep gummies without melatonin; median four words, misspellings kept), so the requirements must be inferred from the query. choice is correct if and only if it is the Exact product, so correctness here is human verdict from the annotations in ASQ. For the evaluations in this paper, we start from portion of the SQID test split, keep products with product-specific image, and call query eligible if it has at least one Exact and at least nine Substitute or Complement products (3,541 queries). Visiting eligible queries in seeded random order, we build 500 tasks, each with (a) one Exact product as the target, chosen at random when the query has several (median five), and (b) nine distractors from the same querys judged list. More details about the dataset and our evaluation process are in Sec. of the Supplement. Each product carries its title, bullet features, description and image, so the task is pure product identification. Because the ground truth is subjective human annotation rather than strict check against objective requirements, some Exact labels are debatable. We treat this label noise as property of the benchmark: it lowers success for every model and leaves comparisons between models and effort settings intact. Wayfair WANDS. WANDS [8], the Wayfair Annotation Dataset, provides 480 real queries from furniture and home-goods retailer, 42,994 products and 233k human labels that grade each queryproduct pair as Exact, Partial or Irrelevant under written guidelines. It changes the retailer, the product domain and the modality at once: products come without images, prices or options, and the published text is lowercased and tokenized (oletto pull down single handle kitchen faucet), so models decide from text alone. Queries are again short search strings (full bed with trundle, 7qt slow cooker, 3 1/2 inch drawer pull; median three words) spanning 159 product classes from accent chairs to bathroom faucets. The correct choice is the Exact product. WANDS judges far more products per query than ESCI (median 247, of which about 24 are Exact and 141 Partial), so we can be stricter about distractors: query is eligible if it has at least one Exact and at least nine Partial products, which 350 of the 480 queries satisfy; 330 form the test set and 20 are held out as pilot. From the WANDS dataset, we build the following tasks for our experiments: for each of the previous queries, we take (a) one Exact product at random as the target and (b) nine Partial products from the same query, i.e. products that annotators judged relevant to the query but not full match, with Irrelevant products never used and (c) Partial products that share name with an Exact product dropped as duplicate listings (affecting 47 tasks). Models see the product name as the title, every catalog attribute as feature: value bullet (median 54 attributes per product with values like upholstery material and overall width) and the description truncated to 1,500 characters. Product class, category and ratings are not shown. As with SQID, the ground truth is human verdict and few Exact labels are hard to defend (the query almost heaven sauna has as its Exact product sauna bucket-and-ladle set); such cases again depress absolute success equally for every model and do not affect comparisons. 3.2. Models and effort manipulation We evaluate ten frontier models from six providers: GPT-6 Astra [31], GPT-6.1 Sol [30] and GPT-6 Luna [32] (OpenAI); Claude Fable 5.1 [3] and Claude Opus 5.5 [4] (Anthropic); Gemini 4 Argon [16] and Gemini 3.1 Pro [15] (Google); DeepSeek V4.1 Flash [10]1; Qwen 3.8 Max [34] (Alibaba); and Kimi K3 [25] (Moonshot). All are queried through the OpenRouter API [33] with identical prompts and shared output budget of 16,000 tokens for reasoning plus answer. Reasoning effort is set with the OpenRouters reasoning.effort parameter at low, medium, or high2. Sampling settings are the provider defaults. Prompt and response. The system prompt casts the model as shopping assistant that must buy the single product, with the right options, that best satisfies the customer. The user message gives the query, the ten products (title, price, features, description, options and image where available) and asks for JSON object with the chosen product number, one value per option type and how confident you are that your chosen product and options satisfy every requirement in the customer instruction, as an integer from 0 (not at all confident) to 10 (completely confident). Of 37,128 responses across the three datasets, 37,099 (99.92%) contained parseable choice and confidence; the rest are dropped. The full prompt is in Sec. of the Supplement. 1We use the DeepSeek Flash series rather than the higher-visibility Pro series because the Pro models are not multimodal. 2We checked that the reasoning.effort parameter is not ignored by the benchmarked models OpenRouter APIs. Additionally, we note DeepSeek V4.1 and Kimi K3 which allow only low and high reasoning. 3 3.3. Metrics and statistical analysis Success rate, confidence and overconfidence. We refer to the proportion of correctly-answered queries among all queries answered by certain LLM at certain effort level as the success rate for that effort level. We will report success rates by model and effort level and 95% confidence intervals on their paired changes across effort levels. Confidence is the integer from 0 to 10 that the model attaches to its answer; we will report its mean per model and effort level with 95% confidence intervals on its paired changes across effort levels. In figures and tables, we rescale the confidence to 0100 scaling so that it can be compared to the success rate. Lastly, we let overconfidence be the difference between the rescaled confidence and the success rate, which we will also report by model and effort level. Calibration metrics. Since the confidence is between 1 and 10, we can rescale using c/10 and treat it as probability. The expected calibration error (ECE) [17, 28] is the average absolute gap between stated confidence and realized success rate across the eleven confidence levels, weighted by how often each level is used; the Brier score [5] is the mean squared gap between c/10 and the 0/1 outcome, which penalizes both miscalibration and inaccuracy; and the AUROC [18] is the probability that randomly chosen correct answer carries higher confidence than randomly chosen wrong one, which measures only whether confidence ranks right above wrong, regardless of its level (Sec. 4.3, Tab. 2). model can have poor ECE and good AUROC if its confidence is informative but uniformly too high. Effect of effort. For every model and every effort-level pair (lowmedium, mediumhigh, lowhigh), we take the tasks answered under both settings, compute the within-task difference in success and confidence, and test whether mean difference differs from zero with paired t-test, reporting the mean with 95% confidence interval (Sec. 4.2). Shared errors. For each effort level, we take the tasks answered by all models at that level (n = 10 at low and high; 8 at medium) and count, for each task, how many of the models chose wrong  (Fig. 3)  , which we denote by k. If the models errors were independent, this count would follow binomial distribution, Binomial(n, p), with the mean error rate p, tightly concentrated around np. We compare the observed distribution of the count to this independence baseline in three ways: (a) the number of tasks that all models fail or all solve, observed versus expected; (b) the variance ratio, the variance of the observed count divided by the variance under independence, which is 1 if errors are independent and grows as errors become shared; and (c) the pairwise error correlation ρ = (cid:0)Var(k)/(p(1 p)) n(cid:1)/(cid:0)n(n 1)(cid:1) (where the Var is taken across tasks) the correlation between any two models error indicators that would produce the observed variance. We also report the KullbackLeibler (KL) divergence of the observed distribution from the binomial baseline. Finally, on tasks where at least two models erred, we ask what share of the wrong choices fall on the single most-chosen wrong product, against Monte-Carlo baseline in which each wrong model picks uniformly among the nine distractors (Sec. 4.4). 4. Results Due to page limit constraints, some figures in this section show only results from the WebShop dataset; the corresponding figures for SQID and WANDS are in Secs. and of the Supplement and are referenced where the text discusses them. The tables cover all three datasets. 4.1. Overview Figure 1 and Fig. S8 show every models success, confidence and reasoning-token usage at the three effort levels on WebShop. We see that success lines are nearly flat and cross each other, confidence lines are nearly all rising, and token usage can differ by two orders of magnitude between providers. Within dataset, models are spread over 411 points, and the ordering is only partly stable: success ranks agree closely between WebShop and SQID, but not between either of WebShop-or-SQID and WANDS. Perhaps this is because WANDS is text-only while WebShop and SQID are multimodal with both images and text. The right panel of Fig. 1 shows that reasoning effort affects the actual number of tokens model uses very unevenly. On WebShop, models like Qwen 3.8 Max and the Gemini models vary more drastically in number of reasoning tokens for each effort level. In contrast, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and both Claude models only slightly increase their token usage with higher reasoning efforts. The same pattern holds on the other two datasets. The middle panel of Fig. 1 shows gap in stated confidence that recurs throughout our results. On WebShop, the two Claude models report mean confidence of about 8 out of 10, while the other eight models report between 8.7 and 9.7. Measured against their success rates, those eight models are overconfident by 7 to 16 percentage points, whereas the two Claude models are slightly underconfident (2.8 and 6.7 points for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5). This gap will reappear later in the calibration metrics (Sec. 4.3). 4.2. Takeaway: At every effort level, the bimodal distribution of the errors indicates that models tend to fail together on the same tasks. the product type and headline attribute but fails secondary constraint such as size, scent or price. On SQID, it is most often Substitute whose title is nearly identical to the Exact products. Practically, this suggests that agreement among frontier models is weak evidence that shopping decision is correct, and an ensemble or second opinion recovers much less than independent errors would suggest. 5. Discussion Effort buys confidence, not correctness. In this paper, we show that increasing reasoning effort increases confidence but not correctness holds across three agentic shopping benchmarks: WebShop, SQID, and WANDS. One explanation is that product choice is bounded by reading rather than reasoning: the information needed to answer is in the listing, and model that misses secondary constraint or is fooled by near-identical substitute at low effort does not recover it by deliberating longer. second explanation is that long reasoning trace supplies the model with the experience of having checked, which it then reports as confidence. The two cases in which accuracy did respond, Qwen 3.8 Max on WebShop  (Fig. 2)  and GPT-6 Luna on WANDS (Fig. S6 in the Supplement) both delivered the whole gain at the lowmedium step, which suggests that there are tasks sufficiently difficult where, for certain models, the low setting is genuinely insufficient, an increase in effort does help, but the 7 6. Limitations Our tasks isolate the decision by handing the model fixed ten-product list; they do not test search, pagination or multistep navigation, where effort might matter more. Ground truth is imperfect: about 15% of WebShop distractors are arguably acceptable, and the SQID and WANDS labels carry the known noise of crowd relevance judgements, which depresses absolute accuracy for every model and may inflate the apparent error correlation, since mislabeled task counts every model as wrong. Comparisons across models and effort levels within dataset share the same labels and are affected much less. Confidence was elicited once, as an integer 010 in the same JSON as the answer; other elicitation protocols [38, 41] might yield different levels, though the stability of rankings across three datasets suggests the model differences are robust. Each condition was run once with provider-default sampling, so run-to-run variance is absorbed into the task-level noise of the paired tests rather than estimated separately. Finally, the effort control is provider-defined abstraction whose implementation varies, as the token counts show; our results describe the control as users experience it, not fixed amount of computation. 7. Conclusion We built evaluations for agentic shopping from three benchmark datasets. We then asked ten frontier LLMs to choose and rate their confidence at low, medium, and high reasoning levels. On every dataset, effort had little effect on accuracy while it significantly raised stated confidence for several models; calibration was stable attribute of the model, with two models near-calibrated or slightly overconfident and the rest substantially overconfident at every setting; and models failed together far more often than chance, usually on the same wrong product. Thus, for agentic shopping, choosing calibrated model matters more than turning up its effort, and neither its confidence nor its agreement with other agents is reliable guard against error. Future work should test whether the pattern persists when the agent also searches, whether training for calibration transfers to this setting, and whether the shared errors we observe stem from shared training data, shared listing cues, or both. The ranking of models by overconfidence barely changes between different datasets between which accuracy ranges often differ by almost forty percentage points (Fig. S1 in the Supplement). Reasoning effort does not break this correlation: the models are as aligned in their mistakes at high effort as at low. Implications for evaluation. Effort settings are often believed to improve the accuracy of decision tasks. However, in agentic shopping, increasing thinking effort doe little for accuracy but significantly increases the models reported confidence. Thus, evaluations of agentic systems should report calibration and effort-conditioned results alongside accuracy, use paired designs with multiple-comparison control (8 of our 11 nominally significant accuracy effects disappear under correction; see Tab. sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: Large language models were used in this work in two distinct roles. First, as the objects of study: the ten commercial models listed in Sec. 3.2 were queried through the OpenRouter API to produce the product choices, confidence ratings and reasoning-token counts analyzed in the paper; their outputs are data, not contributions to the manuscript. Second, as research and writing aid: an LLM-based coding assistant (Anthropics Claude, accessed through the Cursor editor) was used to help write and debug the Python code for task construction, scoring, statistical analysis and figure and table generation, and to draft and edit the text of this paper, including the related-work discussion, from the authors experimental design, results and notes. All experimental decisions, the analysis plan, the interpretation of results and the final text were made and verified by the authors, who reviewed every number against the raw data and take full responsibility for the content. No generative AI tool was used to create or alter images or to fabricate data or citations.

The mean confidence on wrong answers is much lower for Claude models than for non-Claude ones, and the 95% intervals are narrow relative to these gaps. confidence threshold that would catch most of these models errors would also discard most of their correct answers; for the Claude models, threshold around 8 separates the two populations far better.
